rows.source_quote: Saudi-backed forces entered the Aden governorate on Wednesday and the local Giants Brigades seized control of the city, pledging allegiance to the PLC and flying the national flag of Yemen on official buildings for the first time in years.

rows.comments: The article was published on Friday, 9 January 2026, so 'On Wednesday' refers to 7 January. The PLC is described earlier as 'Yemen's internationally recognised government.' The source says the PLC 'accused' Zubaidi of high treason and referred him to the prosecutor general with a formal investigation launched, which supports the claim's use of 'charged.' The name 'Zoubaidi' vs 'Zubaidi' is a transliteration variant.
rows.source_quote: On Wednesday, the PLC, of which the STC is part of, stripped Zubaidi of his membership and accused him of "high treason".

rows.comments: The source confirms armed clashes broke out on Sept. 16 in northwest Sanaa between Houthi militias and army units. The mention of 'four days of fighting' starting Sept. 16 straightforwardly implies the fighting continued into the following day and beyond.
rows.source_quote: This indeed happened on Sept. 16, when armed clashes broke out in northwest Sanaa between the movement's militias and some army units. After four days of fighting, Gen. Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar carried out what could be described as a coup attempt against President Abed Rabbo Mansour Hadi.

rows.comments: The source confirms mass Houthi demonstrations in Sanaa in August 2014, pressure on President Hadi to reverse fuel subsidy cuts, calls for the government to resign, meetings between Houthi and government representatives, and the Houthis' rejection of the government's offer (which left out the fuel subsidy reversal). The claim's characterization of concessions as 'insufficient' is a fair paraphrase of the Houthis rejecting an offer that omitted their key demand.
rows.source_quote: Tens of thousands of Yemenis massed in the capital Sanaa on Friday in a protest called by the Shi'ite Houthi movement, which wants the government to reverse a decision on cutting fuel subsidies and resign. ... Representatives from the Houthis and the government had met on Thursday to try to reach an agreement to defuse tensions. ... The Houthis rejected that

rows.comments: The source confirms that airline companies suspended flights to Sanaa, as announced by the Civil Aviation and Meteorology Authority. The claim's phrasing 'into and out of' is a reasonable paraphrase of the suspension, as airlines suspending service to Sanaa would affect both inbound and outbound flights.
rows.source_quote: The Civil Aviation and Meteorology Authority announced late Thursday evening that Arab and foreign airline companies decided to suspend their flights to Sanaa.

rows.comments: The source confirms 60 killed in clashes on 19 September and notes the death toll was expected to rise, but it does not definitively state that more than 60 were killed. The claim asserts 'more than 60' as fact, while the source only says the toll 'has risen to 60' with an expectation it could increase.
rows.source_quote: The death toll from deadly clashes between Yemeni army forces and Shiite Houthi militants in northern Sanaa has risen to 60, a security source said Friday. ... The source expected the death toll to rise as scores were injured in the deadly violence.

rows.comments: The source confirms that on that evening, the UN secretary-general's envoy to Yemen announced an agreement to resolve the crisis. However, the source does not name the envoy as 'Benomar' — it only refers to 'the UN secretary-general's envoy to Yemen.' The core event described in the claim is supported, but the specific identification of the envoy as Benomar cannot be confirmed from this source text alone.
rows.source_quote: On the evening of Sept. 20, the UN secretary-general's envoy to Yemen announced that an agreement had been reached to resolve the current crisis in Yemen based on the results of the National Dialogue Conference.

rows.comments: The source supports the claim that al-Ahmar's (Ahmer's) forces fought the Houthis and then surrendered. However, the source does not specifically mention the Houthis taking over 'the offices of the prime minister, the state television building, and military headquarters.' It only generally states that 'it took northern Yemen Shiite rebels a couple of days to take over key government buildings and military buildings,' without specifying which buildings.
rows.source_quote: Just this week, his loyalists briefly fought the Houthis before surrendering.

rows.comments: The source states the capital was pronounced under Houthi control 'on Sunday,' nearly a month after rallies began on 18 August. Counting forward, that Sunday falls on 21 September 2014, matching the claim's date. The claim's wording 'declared themselves in control' is a reasonable paraphrase of 'pronounced as being under control of the Houthi rebels.'
rows.source_quote: The Yemeni capital was pronounced as being under control of the Houthi rebels on Sunday - nearly a month after the beginning of their massive rallies in the capital.

rows.comments: The source states that Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar 'seems to have managed to escape' after Houthis seized his headquarters, which aligns with the claim that the general was believed to have escaped capture. The hedged language ('seems to have') matches the claim's 'was believed to have.'
rows.source_quote: the group's fighters had seized the headquarters of the 1st armored division, led by Major General Ali Mohsen al-Ahmar, who seems to have managed to escape

rows.comments: The source supports that Hadi nominated bin Mubarak as PM and that the Houthis rejected/vetoed the choice. It also confirms Houthis occupied key buildings in Sanaa. However, the source does not mention a government call for Houthis to turn over key points to security forces, does not describe the Houthis as keeping a 'firm grip on the government,' and does not name Basindawa as the PM being replaced (though it does mention the previous PM resigned).
rows.source_quote: A decree appointed Ahmed Awad bin Mubarak to the post, but rebels said the matter was "under consultation". ... rebel spokesman Abdul Malik al-Ijri said that his group did not agree with the appointment and that consultation on a new prime minister was still ongoing.

rows.comments: Most elements of the claim are supported: the Houthis signed an accord, refused to sign an annex calling for the state to retake seized areas and return captured weapons, and Hadi declared an immediate ceasefire urging all parties to implement the agreement. However, the claim states the deal 'prompted' Basindawa to resign, implying the signing came first and caused the resignation. The source says he resigned 'Hours before the signing ceremony,' though he did cite the accord as his reason. Additionally, the claim says the deal was with 'the government,' while the source says 'other political parties.'
rows.source_quote: Hours before the signing ceremony Prime Minister Mohammed Basindwa submitted his resignation to President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi, saying he hoped the move would help consensus emerge from the accord.

rows.comments: The source confirms that Al Jazeera received audio recordings of Saleh coordinating with a Houthi leader, which supports the claim that the conversations indicated Saleh aided the Houthis. The recordings were from October, a month after the Houthis took control of Sanaa, so 'aided the Houthis in their takeover' is a slight simplification, but the core assertion is well-supported.
rows.source_quote: In the audio recording, received by Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Saleh is heard apparently coordinating military and political moves with Abdul Wahid Abu Ras, a Houthi leader.

rows.comments: The source confirms that Houthis kidnapped bin Mubarak in January 2015 and that they were applying pressure on Hadi's government (ministers under house arrest, Hadi announcing resignation under Houthi pressure). However, the source does not mention the motive of gaining control over the drafting of a new constitution, nor does it mention a 'unity government.' The source instead notes that bin Mubarak had been nominated as prime minister and his appointment was rejected by the Houthis.
rows.source_quote: Houthi rebels have freed President Abd-Rabbu Mansour Hadi's chief of staff, whose abduction set in motion days of political turmoil in Yemen. ... Several ministers under Hadi remain on house arrest. Hadi announced last week that he would leave office under Houthi pressure.

rows.comments: The source confirms that Saleh's GPC pulled out of the unity cabinet led by Hadi and PM Khaled Bahah, and that events occurred in November. However, it contradicts the claim that the GPC 'joined the Houthis' in a boycott: the source states that rebel representatives (including Houthis) 'committed to support' the government, not boycott it. Only the GPC's withdrawal is mentioned.
rows.source_quote: The UN sanctions prompted Saleh to pull his General People's Congress party out of the just-formed unity cabinet ... Rebel representatives and their rivals, the Sunni Al-Islah (Reform) Islamic party, mandated Hadi to form a government and committed to support it.

rows.comments: The source supports that Houthi rebels shelled Hadi's residence and laid siege to the presidential palace, and that Hadi, Bahah, and the cabinet resigned in protest. However, several claim details are unsupported or contradicted: (1) the shelling of Hadi's home occurred 'on Wednesday' (Jan 21), not January 20; (2) the source says rebels 'laid siege to' the palace, not 'captured' it; (3) the source makes no mention of September 2014 or actions from which rebels had previously refrained.
rows.source_quote: Earlier this week, Houthi gunmen fired on Mr Bahah's convoy and then laid siege to the presidential palace, where he was staying. Then on Wednesday the home of President Hadi was shelled, shattering a ceasefire that had been agreed only hours earlier.

rows.comments: The source says the ultimatum was issued TO Major General Stepanov by an activist (a driver), not BY Stepanov to the government. The threat was that Stepanov himself would be torn to pieces if he did not comply, not that Russians would tear Chechens to pieces. The claim reverses the direction of the ultimatum and the target of the threat.
rows.source_quote: Один из активистов, шофер автотранспортной конторы, предъявил ультиматум находившемуся в обкоме начальнику местного военного авиационного училища генерал-майору Степанову: либо выйти к толпе и выступить перед ней с заявлением о том, что чеченцы будут выселены из Грозного, либо быть через несколько минут растерзанным.

rows.comments: The source clearly supports the claim that Maskhadov attempted to attract foreign investment in Chechnya's oil industry and the reconstruction of Grozny. However, the source does not mention Maskhadov trying to 'concentrate power in his hands to establish authority' or having 'trouble creating an effective state or a functioning economy.' While the source notes Chechnya is 'independent but ruined' and plagued by kidnappings, it does not frame these as Maskhadov's personal struggles with state-building or power concentration.
rows.source_quote: If half of the president's visit is for public relations purposes, the other is to clinch deals to reconstruct Grozny, to invest in Chechen oil and create a viable economy.

rows.comments: The source text contains the exact phrase matching the claim, in the context of kidnappings in Chechnya.
rows.source_quote: But victims are rarely killed.

rows.comments: The source supports that Ukrainians fled the Holodomor to Chechnya and that Chechens provided food and shelter, and that some settled permanently (e.g., Lyuba 'ended up spending the rest of her life among her adoptive people'). However, the claim's assertion that 'the Soviet government threatened' people not to help Ukrainians and that Chechens 'did not follow Soviet orders' is completely absent from the source. The source mentions Stalin's order to seal off Ukrainian territory but says nothing about threats against those offering aid. The term 'Chechen-Ingush ASSR' is also not used in the source.
rows.source_quote: Some Ukrainians fleeing starvation escaped to the southeast, where Chechens extended their hospitality. ... While many other Holodomor refugees tried to reach neighboring Romania or Poland, the family instead chose to head southeast to Soviet-ruled Chechnya, whose residents were then rumored to offer food and shelter to starving Ukrainians.

rows.comments: The source confirms the house is called 'Ginger and Fred' after dancers Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, and that it represents a pair of dancers. However, the source does not attribute the naming to Gehry specifically, nor does it state he 'originally' called it that. The source presents the name as a general nickname without specifying who coined it.
rows.source_quote: It represents two dancers Fred Astair and Ginger Rogers � that�s why it�s also called �Ginger and Fred� .

rows.comments: The article is dated 10-26-98 and says Bargishev was killed 'yesterday,' confirming October 25, 1998. The source confirms Bargishev was Chechnya's top anti-kidnapping official, killed by a remote-controlled bomb, that colleagues vowed to continue their offensive, and that other officials blamed the attack on his success in freeing hostages including 24 Russian soldiers and an English couple. The claim's attribution of the campaign to 'President Maskhadov' is a slight elaboration—the source mentions Maskhadov's office issued a statement and that Bargishev was to launch the offensive, but does not explicitly say Maskhadov personally started the campaign.
rows.source_quote: Chechnya's top anti-kidnapping official was killed yesterday when a bomb tore his car to pieces on the day he was to launch a major offensive on hostage-takers in the breakaway republic. ... Bargishev's colleagues insisted they would not be intimidated by the attack and would go ahead with their offensive. ... Other anti-kidnapping officials blamed the attack on Bargishev's recent success in securing the release of several hostages, including 24 Russian soldiers and an English couple.

rows.comments: The source confirms that the 'Fred and Ginger' name was Gehry's idea, and that he was 'afraid to import American Hollywood kitsch to Prague,' which led to the name being dropped. The claim's paraphrase of 'discarded his own idea' is a straightforward implication of this passage.
rows.source_quote: That was Frank's idea but then he was afraid to import American Hollywood kitsch to Prague, though we said Fred and Ginger were artists.

rows.comments: The source confirms that a restaurant called 'Ginger & Fred' exists on the 7th floor of the Dancing House. However, the claim's assertion that the nickname is 'now mainly used' for the restaurant (implying a shift from prior usage, likely referring to the building itself) is not addressed by the source. The source simply describes the restaurant without discussing the history or evolution of the nickname's usage.
rows.source_quote: that is the Ginger & Fred Restaurant on the 7th floor of the Dancing House.

rows.comments: The source, dated September 2016, confirms all elements of the claim: two floors converted over five months into a 21-room hotel operated by Luxury Suites s.r.o. It also confirms apartments in towers named Ginger Royal Suite and Fred Royal Suite, the Ginger & Fred restaurant on the seventh floor, the Glass Bar on the eighth floor, and the Dancing House Gallery in the building.
rows.source_quote: A new 21-room four-star hotel has opened in the Dancing House in Prague. Two floors that had previously been used as an art gallery were converted over five months into hotel rooms ... The hotel is operated by Luxury Suites s.r.o.

rows.comments: The source supports the claim that AJMN receives public funding (also described as 'state-funded' and 'the Qatari government has provided the majority of its funding'). However, the source says nothing about AJMN being chartered as a 'private foundation for public benefit' under Qatari law. That specific characterization is absent from the article.
rows.source_quote: Al Jazeera told the Washington Examiner that the outlet operates with editorial independence while receiving public funding, similar to global media organizations such as the British Broadcasting Company, among others.

rows.comments: The source confirms that Fred Astaire is represented by a rock tower and Ginger Rogers by a glass tower. However, the claim that the tower 'includes a metal head' is not supported — the source only mentions 'imaginary hair' on top of the male tower, with no mention of metal.
rows.source_quote: The male part of the dancing couple is represented by a rock tower and the woman is symbolized by a tower made of glass. The top of the male tower is covered with imaginary hair.

rows.comments: The source confirms that Al-Jazeera received funding from the Qatari government and is considered a private company. However, the claim's specific assertion that AJMN is chartered as a 'private foundation for public benefit' under Qatari law is not mentioned anywhere in the source. The source describes it as 'a private company, not a government station,' which is related but not the same legal designation. Additionally, the source uses past tense ('began operations with' funding) rather than confirming ongoing receipt of public funding.
rows.source_quote: Al-Jazeera began operations with millions of dollars in funding from the Qatari government. It is not yet financially independent but is considered a private company, not a government station.

rows.comments: The source directly states that the Qatar Council of Ministers (i.e., the cabinet) nominates Al Jazeera's leaders, who are then appointed by the ruler of Qatar (i.e., the emir). This matches the claim closely.
rows.source_quote: allowing the network to receive funding from the Qatar Council of Ministers, which nominates Al Jazeera's leaders, who the ruler of Qatar then appoints.

rows.comments: The Guardian article itself is a media outlet arguing that Qatar exercises editorial influence over Al Jazeera's content, detailing a specific incident of editorial intervention ordered by a Qatar-based news director to prioritize the Qatari emir's speech. The article also notes broader consolidation of Qatari control over the channel.
rows.source_quote: Al-Jazeera's editorial independence has been called into question after its director of news stepped in to ensure a speech made by Qatar's emir to the UN led its English channel's coverage of the debate on Syrian intervention.

rows.comments: The source confirms that an 'independent public corporation' called 'The Al Jazeera Satellite Network' was established by Law No. 1 of 1996. However, the source does not mention a launch date of 1 November 1996 for the channel, nor does it mention Hamad Bin Khalifa Al Thani as the founder. The law's date is listed as 08/02/1996, and the official gazette publication date is 19/03/1996, but no channel launch date is given. The Emir is not named anywhere in the source text.
rows.source_quote: An independent public corporation with a legal personality called “The Al Jazeera Satellite Network” shall be established and shall have a separate budget.

rows.comments: The source confirms the launch date of November 1, 1996, the initial six hours of daily programming, and the expansion to 24-hour broadcasting on January 1, 1999. However, the source does not mention an increase to 12 hours by the end of 1997, nor does it mention terrestrial signal, cable, satellite distribution, or that satellite was free to users in the Arab world. Those details in the claim are unsupported by this source.
rows.source_quote: November 1, 1996: Al Jazeera channel is launched, transmitting six hours a day. ... January 1, 1999: Al Jazeera expands its schedule to 24 hours a day and is now transmitted in the Middle East, North Africa and Europe.

rows.comments: Every element of the claim is directly supported by the source: Hooker's influence as Hartford's minister, the 1638 sermon inspiring the Fundamental Orders, the Orders establishing civil government and separating Connecticut from Massachusetts, and their serving as the legal basis until Charles II's 1662 charter.
rows.source_quote: As minister of the church in Hartford, Hooker enjoyed enormous influence. ... In 1638, Hooker preached a sermon ... This sermon served as inspiration for the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut , which established a civil government and assured the existence of Connecticut as a separate colony, independent from Massachusetts. The Fundamental Orders served as the legal basis for the Connecticut Colony until Charles II granted it a formal charter in 1662 .

rows.comments: The source directly supports all three components of the claim: Qatari officials considering selling Al Jazeera in 2005 due to Bush administration displeasure, the hiring of Barbour Griffith & Rogers on a $300,000 contract, and the PR campaign's partial success with Republicans appearing on the network. Minor differences: the source does not explicitly call Haley Barbour a 'Republican' or mention 'the Republican side of US politics,' and the word 'boycott' is not used, though 'began booking Republican guests' implies they had not appeared before.
rows.source_quote: By 2005, the Bush administration's displeasure with Al-Jazeera was so intense that it was straining the U.S.'s relationship with Qatar, an important ally in the region, and Qatari officials were considering selling off the station, The New York Times reported . That same year, Qatar hired Barbour Griffith & Rogers, the lobbying and public relations firm founded by Haley Barbour, on a $300,000 contract to improve relations with the Bush administration, according to O'Dwyer's PR Daily. ... "The PR campaign, to a certain degree, was successful," said Suhail Khan, who served in the White House Office of Public Liaison during the Bush administration. "They just began booking Republican guests."

rows.comments: The source confirms that the colony's charter was hidden in the tree, that the monument stands at the corner of Charter Oak Avenue and Charter Oak Place, and that the Charter Oak appeared on the state quarter. However, the source does not mention that the tree was a 'white oak,' does not date the charter to 1662, does not mention an 'English governor-general,' does not reference an 'original settlement area,' and does not call Charter Oak Place a 'historic street.' Several specific details in the claim are thus unsupported by this source.
rows.source_quote: a hollow space in the tree was used to hide the colony's charter ... In 1905, a monument was erected at the location of the fallen oak tree. It stands at the corner of Charter Oak Avenue and Charter Oak Place in Hartford's downtown. ... In 1999 the Charter Oak was chosen as Connecticut's state symbol on the state quarter.

rows.comments: The source confirms the date (December 15, 1814), the five states (Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Vermont), and that secession was discussed. However, the claim oversimplifies the convention's purpose as being specifically about secession, when the source says only 'the more extreme delegates raised the possibility of secession, but others sought only to dictate amendments.' The source also does not mention Maine or its status as part of Massachusetts.
rows.source_quote: Hartford Convention , (December 15, 1814–January 5, 1815), in U.S. history, a secret meeting in Hartford , Connecticut, of Federalist delegates from Connecticut , Rhode Island , Massachusetts , New Hampshire , and Vermont ... The more extreme delegates raised the possibility of secession, but others sought only to dictate amendments to the Constitution that would protect their interests.

rows.comments: The source contradicts the claim on two key points: it dates the formation of the ENLF to March 1985, not April 1984, and it explicitly states that PLOTE remained outside the coalition, meaning the ENLF comprised only LTTE, EPRLF, TELO, and EROS — not all five groups as the claim asserts.
rows.source_quote: In March 1985, the LTTE, EPRLF, TELO, and EROS formed a united front organization, the Eelam National Liberation Front (ENLF). PLOTE, probably the most genuinely Marxist-Leninist of the five major guerrilla groups, remained outside the coalition.

rows.comments: The source does describe the Supreme Court's Sala Penal annulling criminal actions against Asfura and Castillo Cruz, which partially aligns with the claim. However, the article is dated 1 June 2021 and refers to the decision being made 'este martes' (this Tuesday), placing the event around June 2021 — not 15 December 2025 as the claim asserts. The specific date in the claim is contradicted by the source.
rows.source_quote: Redacción El Heraldo 01.06.2021 TEGUCIGALPA, HONDURAS.- La Sala Penal de la Corte Suprema de Justicia (CSJ) determinó este martes declarar 'ha lugar' el recurso de apelación presentado por la defensa del alcalde capitalino Nasry 'Tito' Asfura y la regidora Nilvia Ethel Castillo Cruz

rows.comments: The source supports several key elements: Shevardnadze interrupted his trip to western Georgia, the Abkhazian legislature voted to make Abkhazia a 'sovereign state,' Shevardnadze complained they acted 'without considering the opinion of the majority of Abkhasian population,' and Gamsakhurdia was described as ousted with ongoing unrest in western Georgia. However, the source does not mention the specific date of 23 July, the lack of quorum, the Georgian faction boycotting the session, the term 'Supreme Council,' or 'December 1991 Coup.' These significant details in the claim are absent from the source.
rows.source_quote: Georgian leader Eduard Shevardnadze cut short his tour of western Georgia to return to the capital Tbilisi ... Shevardnadze complained the breakaway faction acted 'without considering the opinion of the majority of Abkhasian population.'

rows.comments: The source article, dated 27 June 2011, discusses the broader international Gaza flotilla and Egypt's agreement to allow cargo unloading at El-Arish, but makes no mention of the French yacht Dignité Al Karama, the island of Kastellorizo, the date 16 July, or any departure toward Alexandria. The claim describes a specific event that is not addressed in this source.

The source confirms that hostages were taken, that Georgian troops were sent to secure the highway and railroad, and that one of every 10 trains had been robbed. However, the claim adds several details not found in the source: that hostages were taken to an 'unknown hiding-place in Abkhazia,' that troops entered specifically 'to free hostages,' that the area was 'loosely controlled by the government due to insurgency,' and that railroads were 'often robbed by unknown bands.' These additions are not supported by the source text.
rows.source_quote: High-level Georgian negotiators, including the Interior Minister and security chief, were taken hostage. Georgian troops sent to secure the highway and railroad, where one of every 10 trains had been robbed, were attacked and at least 30 people were killed.

rows.comments: The source discusses civilian death estimates in overlapping ranges (40,000–120,000, and a plausible estimate of 70,000–90,000), which broadly aligns with the claim's 50,000–100,000 range. However, the source refers to 'civilians' broadly rather than specifically 'Chechens' as an ethnic group, and discusses deaths rather than 'dead or missing' combined. No specific figure of 50,000–100,000 for Chechens dead or missing is stated.
rows.source_quote: So, for the period from 1994 to 2002 estimates range from 40.000 to 120.000 civilians. ... setting the death toll, from the beginning of the first war to present days, at 70.000-90.000 civilians, about 10.000 Russian soldiers and at least the same amount of Chechen rebels, is a plausible (and possibly even a too conservative) estimate.

rows.comments: The source identifies Agnes Gund's parents as George Gund II (father) and Jessica Roesler Gund (mother), matching the claim.
rows.source_quote: her father, George Gund II, was president of the Cleveland Trust Company ... Her mother, Jessica Roesler Gund, oversaw the home

rows.comments: The source is a Human Rights Watch report focused specifically on war crimes during the May 2002 Kisangani mutiny and subsequent RCD crackdown. It does mention a Banyamulenge revolt led by Patrick Masunzu beginning in January 2002, but does not describe the Banyamulenge as 'the backbone of Rwanda's militia forces,' nor does it state they became 'tired of control from Kigali.' The source does not address Rwanda's overall war situation worsening, nor does it mention RCD members giving up fighting or joining Kabila's government. The broader claims about the war's trajectory and RCD defections are not addressed in this report.

The source text does not mention anyone named 'Hemphill' at all. While the article does reference the Deep Sea Conservation Coalition (DSCC) as a coalition that began campaigning for a moratorium against deep-sea mining in 2019, it provides no information about Hemphill's educational background in marine biology, his involvement in regional-scale ocean conservation, or his role as a founding steering committee member of the DSCC.

The source identifies two key issues in the no-confidence motion: failing to prevent an alleged scam in the bond market, and failing to stop anti-Muslim riots. It does not mention 'interference in the Central Bank' as an issue. While the bond market scam may be related to the Central Bank, the source does not characterize the issue as 'interference in the Central Bank.'

The source is an artnet gallery page about Yitzhak Frenkel-Frenel's painting 'A House in Safed.' It contains extensive biographical detail about Frenkel-Frenel but makes no mention of 'Joseph Constant' whatsoever.

rows.comments: The source confirms the UK premiere was in 1985 with Gary Graffman as soloist, and that Wittgenstein commissioned the concerto in 1923 (i.e., the 1920s). However, the source does not explicitly state that Wittgenstein 'played it many times' or that the work 'slipped from the repertoire' — these are reasonable inferences from Wittgenstein's life-long exclusive rights and the 61-year gap between the first performance and the UK premiere, but they are not directly stated.
rows.source_quote: Wittgenstein commissioned the concerto in 1923 and it had its first performance in Vienna on 22nd. September the following year with Korngold himself conducting. Wittgenstein held life-long exclusive rights on this work, which at its UK premiere in 1985 was called a keyboard Salome by the soloist Gary Graffman because of its immense difficulties.

rows.comments: The article describes Cenat's outrage at Lil Nas X for 'disrespecting God' and mocking Christianity, but it never states Cenat's own religious affiliation or identifies him as Catholic. The source discusses Christianity in general terms but does not specify Cenat's denomination.

The source text is a VOA article about Afghan insurgent groups stepping up attacks against the Taliban. It does not mention Massoud, does not mention $8 billion worth of U.S. military equipment seized by the Taliban, and does not describe an NRF operational shift to guerrilla warfare due to seized equipment. None of the claim's key assertions appear in the source.

The source is an article about behind-the-scenes facts of the film 'Love Actually' itself. It does not mention any unofficial remake of Love Actually, nor does it compare the number of love stories between Love Actually and any other film. The claim is entirely unaddressed by the source.

The source mentions executions at San Rafael Cemetery in Málaga, but does not support the specific claims. It says ~4,500 were executed (not ~4,000 who declined to evacuate), and makes no mention of rape, systematic round-ups, or people being 'piled into mass graves.' The claim about Almería's citizens rejecting refugees is entirely absent from the source.
rows.source_quote: Around 4,500 people were executed in San Rafael cemetery by Franco forces in the period 1936 to 1957

rows.comments: The article is dated Dec 31, 2025, so 'last night' refers to December 30, 2025. The title confirms age 76. The source says 'sudden illness' rather than 'short illness,' but this is a reasonable paraphrase.
rows.source_quote: The very first full-time employee of TSR, the company which created D&D, passed away last night after a sudden illness.

rows.comments: The source supports the claim that URY is the oldest independent radio station in the UK (also stating it became the UK's first legal independent radio station in 1968). However, the source is an archived page from 2008 and makes no mention of any 2020 Student Radio Awards Best Station Award. The only award mentioned is BBC Radio One Student Station of the Year 2005.
rows.source_quote: The oldest legal independent radio station in the country, URY is the home of UK student radio.

rows.comments: The source is an Arabic-language article from Al Arabiya about the assassination of Al-Jabal Brigade leader Muharreh al-Jermani in al-Suwayda. It describes his opposition to the Syrian regime, his role in protest movements, and his faction's detention of regime officers to pressure for prisoner releases. The article makes no mention of human rights abuses, repression of protests, forced conscription, or criticism from local activists regarding civil liberties. In fact, the source portrays al-Jermani as a participant in protests against the regime, not as someone repressing them.

The source is a 'Contact' page on CB Forrest's website containing only Twitter contact information and navigation elements. It makes no mention of poetry publications, literary journals, or praise from other writers.

The source supports that clashes occurred in southern Aleppo involving Zaytan/Khalasa, and that pro-regime forces retook these villages after losing them earlier. However, the claim's casualty figure of 'near 86 soldiers killed' contradicts the source's 'at least 70 fighters.' The source says 'fighters,' not 'soldiers.' rows.comments: The source discusses using radiotrophic fungi and melanin-regolith composites as radiation shields, but never mentions 'paints' or 'coating the walls of spacecraft.' The specific application described in the claim is not addressed in the source text.

The source confirms that the Sioux used the plant to treat diarrhea, which is a gastrointestinal illness. However, the claim has two issues: (1) the source does not state that 'First Nations peoples believe that the berry has many health properties' as a general claim — it only describes specific medicinal uses by specific tribes (Salish, Kootenai, Sioux); and (2) the Sioux used the roots, not the berry, to treat diarrhea. The broader characterization of First Nations beliefs about the berry's health properties is not directly supported.
rows.source_quote: The Sioux boiled the roots, strained them through cloth and the tea to cure diarrhea [ 37 ].

rows.comments: The source only lists winners for The Game Awards 2025. It does not provide any cumulative historical data about how many total awards the Final Fantasy series has won across all years of The Game Awards, nor does it make any comparison to other franchises' total award counts. The claim about '10 awards' and 'more than any other franchise' cannot be verified from this single-year winners list.

rows.comments: The source states that 69.7% of fireworks-caused wildfire ignitions were on Native American tribal lands during 1980–2016, not 76.8% as claimed. Additionally, the source does not mention anything about native areas getting 'extra revenue' from fireworks sales. The source does note that fireworks may be sold on tribal lands even when state bans exist, which loosely relates to the 'lessened restrictions' part of the claim, but the specific percentage is contradicted and the revenue claim is unsupported.
rows.source_quote: Of these, the bulk (69.7%) were situated on Native American tribal lands, whereas relatively fewer occurred on public lands (24.6%), privately owned lands (5%), and federally managed areas on tribal land (0.7%).
